d0a311081328f2e0a769614c57c594afb47337f7.summary: JFrog Security Research describes the 'testmetest' campaign: an npm worm and a hidden CI publisher that armed 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners, including accounts of real developers and organizations. It uses a native addon that decrypts a hidden file at runtime, forged commit dates, and execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs. The report links this infrastructure to shellpanel scanning of cPanel systems via CVE-2026-41940, but says downstream compromises are not confirmed. Attribution to the original Miasma operators is not established.

hedges: The report uses 'testmetest campaign' because its evidence shows shared tooling, but does not establish that the original Miasma operators are responsible.
There is not one proven continuous execution chain from every npm infection to CVE exploitation.
No evidence confirms successful exploitation of downstream cPanel systems, so scanner targets are not counted as victims.
Whether Git credentials were harvested after compromise is described as an inference that remains unproven.
The most likely explanation for the Wedding repository infection is stolen collaborator access rather than compromise of the ismahhaziq account itself.
The recovered ci.js code establishes the intended automated mechanism, not that this particular release used it.
The metadata-only review cannot establish downstream victim identities, the number of affected systems, or the envelopes' plaintext contents.
Listing a package in the campaign inventory does not make its benign releases malicious.

d02941ad349dc5ff4e9692fd3181a8f7047d49c6.summary: Trend Micro's TrendLabs blog (published 2011-10-05) describes the Android backdoor ANDROIDOS_ANSERVER.A, which arrives as a fake e-book reader app from a third-party Chinese app store. It uses an encrypted blog site as a backup command-and-control channel and has two hardcoded C&C servers. Eighteen binaries were uploaded to the blog between July 23 and September 26. Later versions show fake update prompts and try to terminate four security apps.

d01e8492eb25e3a9dfa0218367a708d2d3230c93.summary: Sygnia incident-response case study of a 2023 client intrusion attributed to BlackCat (ALPHV) or one of its affiliates. Initial access came through a compromised third-party vendor. The attacker spent weeks moving laterally with Cobalt Strike and proxy tools, exfiltrated data with Rclone to cloud storage, and extorted the victim by email. Encryption was prevented when the client blocked internet access. A CVE id is mentioned in the text but is split across a line break, so it is not recorded.

d024ba07693e90631f56e0ccf049775a082516ca.summary: An educational blog tutorial on a Windows persistence technique: hijacking a default file association so a chosen program runs when a text file is opened. The report says the technique is used by the SILENTTRINITY framework and the Kimsuky cyber espionage group. It also says malware was used in a 2019 campaign against Croatian government agencies by unidentified cyber actors. The walkthrough and demo are not reproduced here.

d0d666177b14b04a9202863e5b062a0e5936b161.summary: AhnLab's ASEC analysis team reports signs of AppleSeed malware being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit, in July 2022. The report says AppleSeed is a backdoor mainly used by the Kimsuky group. Lures were disguised purchase-order and approval documents, plus an Excel file named after an expected installation schedule. The Excel file was password-protected and used a macro that shows the body after the user enables content. The macro uses mshta to fetch and run a further script, which installs AppleSeed. Once running, AppleSeed takes commands from a C2 server. AhnLab V3…
